title: My experience experimenting with Claude and Unity game dev as a hobbyist.
author: rcxa
selftext:
I'm taking a break from my (non-game) personal project while I do some office renovations and I've been really curious about AI game dev from what I've seen here since the Claude 5.5 models came out.

I've had a project I thought about roughly 10 years ago when I was learning programming language construction. Essentially, where the player programs space ships using a BASIC-style language. Every couple of years I'd think about prototyping it so I'd return to my little design document, make some revisions then try build it out but I never got very far with it.

I thought this might be an interesting project to try out with Claude since I have a good understanding of how things like the programming language interpretation should work but it was too time consuming to try to build it in a performant way given that I don't have much time to devote to a project like this. And outside of the gameplay elements, the visuals can pretty much all be done procedurally or are just hard surface modeling.

The foundation is essentially the design document that I've updated periodically throughout the years. For actually prototyping I started by feeding in that document and describing how I envision the intro sequence which is the attached video. To gauge whether I thought Claude was understanding the concept I had it output the intro sequence as essentially a movie script so I could read through and see what it got wrong and steer it until reading the document aligned with what I was imagining (minus the dialogue which I'll return to).

Once I had the design document and intro sequence script I set up a blank Unity project and set up the baseline guidance. That baseline guidance defines the architecture and the sort of "contract" between Claude and me working on this project. A lot of that is personal preference and was defined largely by pointing it to one of my larger game repos and describing that I learned Unity from Code Monkey and try to stick that guidance as much as I can. I don't let Claude make basic architectural decisions like stack (in this case Unity with Blender for model generation) and code organization. I think it does a good job if it understands the architectural considerations for the project but I find it takes pretty much the same amount of time to define the architecture as it does those considerations, plus I'm familiar with Unity, I can judge it's output better in Unity, and I want to be able to build quickly while still being able to navigate the codebase.

Outside of that, unlike web development, it's not easy to judge whether gameplay is "correct" when working with AI tooling. Two approaches I'm taking towards addressing this are a heavy emphasis on tuning and scenarios.

For tuning, it's basically we need make very heavy use of private serialized fields and scriptable objects. This way, if the output is what I asked for but just feels bad I can try tuning variables until it feels good or until I determine that the ask was bad. This also creates architectural backpressure on the agent, it doesn't use magic numbers that impact gameplay because it's constrained by "tunability".

For scenarios, each moment of gameplay or mechanic has it's own scenario that lets me test it in isolation (stopping the ship from rotating, stopping the lateral movement of the ship, navigating to a waypoint, or just a sandbox where I can build ships and program them, etc.) This also lets me do A/B testing, if there's 2 or more approaches to a mechanic just create a scenario for each, I test each scenario and pick the best option or return to the design phase.

Once all of that guidance was put in place (no code written yet) I ensured that I could connect Claude up to the Unity MCP server and the Blender MCP and started building. Maybe a few things of note on the Blender MCP server:

* The agent must explain to me why it designed the model the way that it did.
* The agent must greybox the model before it generates the candidate model.
* The agent must pass the model to a subagent with the description of the model and the model to evaluate it before it passes the model to me.

I have been very impressed so far with the output so far. There are things about the intro sequence that I think are pretty bad, the two big ones are dialogue and UI.

On dialogue, the agent just Flanderized my guidance on the dialogue. It leaned way to heavy into minor details to create dialogue that just seems unnatural. I'm ignoring that for right now because I want to have it build out tooling for me to author the dialogue/cutscenes myself.

On the UI, it's just kind of totally uninspired. And like the dialogue, the guidance to "draw attention to UI elements" made that gnarly yellow throbbing effect which is more distracting than drawing attention. I have a few ideas for unique UI designs but the goal was rapidly prototyping while I have limited time to invest in the project. I also didn't really want to fix these issues before recording the intro because I think it really demonstrates the issues that arise that are easy to fix but also easy to overlook.

Two closing notes: 

* The most interesting thing that I found is that **the original concept just isn't really that fun**. Playing through the intro feels pretty good, but the rest of what the game was meant to be completely falls apart. The cool thing is I can see if there's a way to make it fun, but this is a prototype that either would have never been made or would have been discarded without the surrounding workflow that allowed it to be built quickly.
* For people that care about this type of stat, I'm 43 PRs deep which represents roughly 17 days where I put in some effort around work and life.

comments.author: Relevant_Science9679
comments.body:
It's quite something for all of us dev to be able to go back to unfinished projects, did the same for a project I spent probably between 600-1000 hours of learning pixel art and making an engine (terraria meet the infinite world of minecraft meet stardew valley). AI refactored my sloppy code, fixed some bugs, updated some UI lib that was crap in monogame and then I was like "ok but this game is never gonna be fun and it has been done since" => next

It was quite cathartic tho to finish some tasks that were left open.

replies.author: TokyoRPGFactory
replies.body: Yeah I get tired of people calling AI code slop, when the AI  found a way to make my game run at twice the FPS because I wasn't precaching graphics right or something

replies.author: Relevant_Science9679
replies.body: Lot of people are lagging behind with the thought of AI being the exchange they have in gemini or chatGPT. For people using it in their daily job, seing the ability to do 5 days of works from a few years ago in 20 minutes perfectly without any bugs, finding other bugs that you hadn't found, you understand it's just a new paradigm. People may like or not like it, there is no going back, why spend 5 days doing something that has no value when you can make progress and focus on what does have value.

replies.author: rcxa
replies.body: Yeah, it was really awesome seeing that sequence on screen for the first time after all of the partial prototypes. Not because it's gonna be an actual game, but just to finally play through it.
